In *KGLens: Towards Efficient and Effective Knowledge Probing of Large Language Models with Knowledge Graphs* (ACL 2024 Workshop Towards Knowledgeable Language Models) [[1]](#ref-1), [Shangshang Zheng](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=MIcmEaMAAAAJ) et al. at Apple tackle a practical problem: large language models confidently state wrong facts, and checking every fact by hand is impossibly expensive.

> Large Language Models (LLMs) might hallucinate facts, while curated Knowledge Graph (KGs) are typically factually reliable especially with domain-specific knowledge. Measuring the alignment between KGs and LLMs can effectively probe the factualness and identify the knowledge blind spots of LLMs. However, verifying the LLMs over extensive KGs can be expensive. In this paper, we present *KGLens, a Thompson-sampling-inspired framework aimed at effectively and efficiently measuring the alignment between KGs and LLMs*. KGLens features a *graph-guided question generator for converting KGs into natural language*, along with a *carefully designed importance sampling strategy based on parameterized KG structure to expedite KG traversal*. Our simulation experiment compares the brute force method with KGLens under six different sampling methods, demonstrating that our approach achieves superior probing efficiency. Leveraging KGLens, we conducted in-depth analyses of the factual accuracy of *ten LLMs across three large domain-specific KGs from Wikidata, composing over 19K edges, 700 relations, and 21K entities*. Human evaluation results indicate that KGLens can assess LLMs with a level of accuracy nearly equivalent to that of human annotators, *achieving 95.7% of the accuracy rate*.

## Methods

Their approach pairs the model with a *knowledge graph*, a structured database of facts, each written as a subject-relation-object triple like "Paris — capital of — France." Each such fact is called an *edge* in the graph. KGLens turns those edges into test questions and asks the model. A smart sampling strategy, inspired by a classical technique called Thompson sampling [[4]](#ref-4), keeps track of which facts the model seems to be weakest on and concentrates future questions there. The result: the team can map out a model's factual blind spots in far fewer questions than asking about every fact one by one.

What makes Thompson sampling special is that it doesn't always test what looks worst right now; it samples from its current belief about each fact, so facts it is unsure about still get tried and the estimates keep improving. Those beliefs are stored as a *beta distribution* per fact, a compact shape that captures both "how often does the model get this fact wrong" and "how sure are we about that estimate" in one object, and updates naturally every time a question is answered.

![How KGLens works. The system starts with a knowledge graph where every fact (edge) carries a running estimate of how often the model gets it wrong. Each round, it picks a batch of facts (preferring the ones the model seems weakest on), turns them into natural-language questions, asks the model, and updates each fact's failure estimate based on the answer. Over time the sampler zeroes in on the model's weakest facts. Figure 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure1.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="figure1-full.png"}

## Results

Across three knowledge graphs built from Wikidata (covering countries, movies, and the NBA, with more than 19,000 facts and 21,000 entities between them), KGLens tested ten LLMs and produced two kinds of result.

The first is evidence that the smart sampling actually saves questions. Figure 3 runs a simulation on the NBA graph. Each fact is given a hidden true "failure probability" (how often the model would get it wrong if asked repeatedly), and KGLens has to recover those probabilities from as few test questions as possible. On the hardest 200 and 600 facts, Thompson sampling and a related strategy called epsilon-greedy (both of which preferentially test the facts they think the model is weakest on) get closer to the true probabilities sooner than the brute-force approach of cycling through every fact in turn. The gap is largest when the question budget is small, which is exactly when it matters most.

![Estimation error on the hardest NBA facts as a function of how many questions the model was asked. Thompson sampling and epsilon-greedy (two strategies that preferentially test likely-wrong facts) reach the same error as a brute-force scan with fewer questions, especially early on. Figure 3 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure3.png){fig-align="center"}

The second result is a map of what the model actually knows. Once KGLens has probed enough facts, it can group the results by the *kind* of relation being asked about ("spouse of", "country of citizenship", "position played", and so on) and by the kind of entity involved. The output isn't "the model is X% accurate overall"; it's "the model is reliable on these kinds of facts and unreliable on those." Figure 6 shows this breakdown for GPT-4 on the hardest difficulty setting.

![Per-relation proficiency map for GPT-4 on HARD mode. Color encodes the *zero-sense rate*: the fraction of facts of that type the model never got right, even across repeated trials. Darker means more reliable. Dot size reflects how many facts of that type were in the graph. A map like this, showing exactly where a frontier model is and isn't reliable, is the kind of artifact KGLens makes cheap to produce. Figure 6 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure6.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="figure6-full.png"}

To check that the automated grading was reliable, the authors compared KGLens's verdicts against human judges. The system agreed with humans 95.7% of the time.

## My Notes

- **A per-relation map is a better output shape for deployment decisions than a single score.** Most factuality benchmarks (TruthfulQA [[2]](#ref-2), HaluEval, FActScore) produce a single number: the model is X% accurate on some fixed test set. KGLens produces a *map* instead: a breakdown of which kinds of facts the model handles well and which it doesn't, against a knowledge graph the team can pick to match their actual deployment. For a team deciding whether to trust a model on, say, NBA player facts before shipping a sports product, that map is what they actually need; a single TruthfulQA number doesn't help.

- **The sampling idea is the part most likely to matter beyond this paper.** Every LLM evaluation hits the same wall: there are too many things to test and each test costs money. KGLens's move (track a running estimate of how often the model fails each test, then preferentially retest the ones it seems worst at) is a standard strategy from classical machine learning applied to LLM evaluation. Figure 3 shows it meaningfully cuts the number of questions needed to find a model's weakest facts. The same idea should plug into other expensive evaluations: red-teaming (searching for harmful outputs), jailbreak coverage (finding prompts that bypass safety rules), or capability probing (checking whether a model can do a specific task).

- **It pairs naturally with [SelfReflect](/posts/20260430-selfreflect-internal-distribution/) [[3]](#ref-3).** Both are Apple papers about measuring what LLMs actually know versus what they claim, and they answer adjacent questions. KGLens tells you *which facts* the model has internalized: which kinds of questions it can answer reliably. SelfReflect tells you whether the model can *honestly summarize its own uncertainty* about a given question. A pipeline that uses KGLens to find a model's weak areas and SelfReflect to check whether the model can admit to those weaknesses would be a stronger evaluation than either alone.

- **The 95.7% agreement with human judges deserves close scrutiny.** Deciding automatically whether a model's answer is correct is hard. Models paraphrase, give partial answers, or say something that is technically right but not the exact wording in the knowledge graph. The 95.7% figure is high, but the relevant question is whether the 4.3% disagreement concentrates on a particular kind of fact (time-sensitive ones, ambiguous relations, facts with multiple valid answers). If it does, those cases are where the automated grader is systematically off, and the team can either adjust or route them to a human reviewer.
